outline.h2: Which product discovery technique fits each risk?
outline.answerHint: **Match the technique to the risk that could kill the idea: interviews and fake doors for value, prototype tests for usability, spikes and data audits for feasibility, and reviews and pricing tests for viability.**
points: Toolkit matrix (visual 1 + astext table, all 14 rows; keywordCarrier.count14). Time and sample values: interviews 4 to 6 users, 45 min each (hub + method); prototype test 5 users (NN/g); card sort 15 (NN/g); spike 1 to 2 days (method); others as method with no invented statistics.
Four risks named in one clause with SVPG link (eav 'what the techniques are for'); link the sibling's risk section instead of explaining ownership again (internalTargets fragment).
Torres's fifth category (ethical) in one sentence: for AI features it is where the wrong-answer question lives.
'Product discovery methods' carrier here or in FAQ 2.
Bridge: 'Value comes first in the matrix because it is the risk most teams skip.'

outline.h2: Which techniques test value risk before anything is built?
outline.answerHint: **Five techniques test value risk, and they differ in what they measure: what users already did, what they say, what many say, what they click and, last, what they pay.**
points: Say → do → pay ladder (visual 2 + astext ol). NN/g attitudinal vs behavioral (eav 'say vs do').
Customer interviews: ask about the last time the problem happened, not 'would you use'; 4 to 6 per user group; pass rule (method).
Analytics and support-ticket review: free evidence you already own; output: frequency of the problem.
Opportunity solution tree (Torres, 4 levels): turns interview notes into opportunities, then assumption tests; one paragraph, link producttalk.
One-question survey: sizes a pattern that interviews found; needs traffic (B2B caveat → FAQ 5).
Fake door test (Amplitude): honest follow-up page, waitlist; trap: clicks show curiosity, not commitment; set the click-through bar before launch (forward link to H2 7).

Mass Media Co. (DOWN link 1): a discovery workshop where stakeholders and end users defined the product and mapped the IA and user flows — a group form of interview and mapping; facts only from the case study.
Bridge: 'Once users want it, the question becomes whether they can use it.'

outline.h2: How do you test usability before engineers write code?
outline.answerHint: **Test usability with a clickable prototype and 5 users per round, and use card sorting and tree testing when the risk is where things live rather than how a screen works.**
points: Prototype usability test: 5 users, Figma prototype, task script, pass = most users finish the core task without help (method); NN/g 31% per user (eav, VERIFY).
Card sorting: 15 participants (NN/g); output: groupings and labels users expect.
Tree testing: findability in a proposed hierarchy before launch (NN/g); do not state a sample unless verified.

TradeZella (DOWN link 2): stakeholder sessions, user flows redrawn around the features traders open most, traders tested the design before it went live. Do not attribute the +40% to testing alone; if a result is quoted, use the case study's own wording.
Trap: testing with colleagues or friends instead of the target user.
Bridge: 'A prototype that tests well can still be unbuildable, which is the next risk.'

outline.h2: Which product discovery techniques settle feasibility and data?
outline.answerHint: **Two techniques settle feasibility: an engineering spike that runs real inputs through a quick build, and a data audit that checks the data exists, can be reached, may be used and is labeled.**
points: Engineering spike: owner engineering, 1 to 2 days (method), output known unknowns + estimate; pass = the one question answered on real inputs.
Data audit: one row per use case; permission is a US legal question (CCPA/CPRA, HIPAA for health data) — one clause, link the sibling's AI section rather than restating its data-readiness section.
Trap: prototyping before the spike, so the team tests a concept engineering cannot ship.
Bridge: 'Buildable and usable still leaves the business question.'

outline.h2: How do you check business viability while the idea is still cheap?
outline.answerHint: **Check viability with a stakeholder review of sales, finance, legal and support constraints, and with a pricing test that asks users to commit money or a seat before you build.**
points: Stakeholder viability review: 30–60 minute walkthrough of the concept with sales, finance, legal, support (method); SVPG lists go-to-market, legal, cost to acquire, monetization and brand as viability concerns (eav).
Pricing test: price on the fake-door or landing page, a pre-order or a paid pilot letter for B2B (method); strongest value evidence on the ladder.
AI cost per call as a viability input (one sentence; sibling covers the check).
Bridge: 'AI features need two more techniques, because the answer changes every time.'

outline.h2: Which product discovery techniques change for AI features?
outline.answerHint: **AI features add two techniques: a Wizard of Oz prototype, where a hidden person plays the model so users react to realistic answers, and an evaluation set that scores real model output against a written bar before design starts.**
points: Wizard of Oz (NN/g definition; suited to conversational UIs and learning algorithms); 5 users; tell participants afterward (ethics, one clause).
Evaluation set: real inputs + written good answer + score (method); pass = clears the bar the team wrote.
Wrong-answer harm: link the sibling's AI checks section (#what-changes-in-product-discovery-for-ai-features); do not restate the five checks or the precision/recall paragraph.
LEAD ANGLE 1 here (see leadAngle).
Bridge: 'Every technique above only works if you decide what counts as a pass before it runs.'

outline.h2: How do you set a pass signal before a test runs?
outline.answerHint: **Write a test card before the test: the hypothesis, the technique, the metric and the result that would prove you right, so the team cannot move the bar after the data comes in.**
points: Strategyzer test card, 4 fields (eav); visual 3 filled with a hypothetical (B2B scheduling SaaS for US clinics or restaurants, AI shift-swap suggestion, fake door, click-through bar set in advance). Label as hypothetical; invent no benchmark: the bar is the team's own choice.
Torres: test assumptions, not ideas (one sentence, link assumption-testing glossary).
Unclear result = retest, not pass (method; do not reuse the sibling's 'unknown counts as a no' wording).
Bridge: 'With pass signals written, the next decision is which test to run first.'

outline.h2: In what order should you run product discovery techniques?
outline.answerHint: **Run the cheapest technique that could kill the idea first, and save expensive, strong evidence such as pricing tests and full prototypes for ideas that already passed.**
points: Cost vs evidence scatter (visual 4 + astext table).

Design sprint as a bundle: 5 days, map → sketch → decide → prototype → test with 5 target customers (GV link); the ONE cross-hub link to /services/startups/design-sprint/ (anchor 'design sprint'). Do not rebuild the hub's day table or the sprint vs discovery table.

points: Workshop bundle trays (visual 5 + astext table); eav 'workshop mapping'. Paraphrase, do not copy the hub step bodies. UP link 2 to the hub (fragment #what-happens-during-the-ai-product-discovery-workshop, conditional; plain hub URL otherwise).

faqs.q: How many product discovery techniques should one round use?
faqs.a: Two or three: one for each risk still open, starting with the one that could kill the idea. More techniques in one round slow the decision without adding much evidence.

faqs.q: Are product discovery techniques the same as UX research methods?
faqs.a: No. They overlap on interviews, surveys and usability tests, but discovery also needs feasibility and viability tests such as spikes, data audits and pricing tests. NN/g's framework places 20 UX research methods on 3 dimensions; carry 'product discovery methods' here if not used in H2 1.

faqs.q: Is a fake door test honest to users?
faqs.a: Yes, if the page behind the door says plainly that the feature is not built yet and offers a waitlist or a way to give feedback. Hiding that, or charging for something that does not exist, damages trust.

faqs.q: Can you run product discovery techniques without a designer?
faqs.a: Yes for interviews, analytics review, surveys and spikes. Prototype tests and Wizard of Oz sessions need someone who can build a believable prototype quickly, which is where a design team helps.

faqs.q: Which techniques work for B2B product discovery with few customers?
faqs.a: Interviews, Wizard of Oz or concierge-style pilots and paid pilot letters, because they work with a handful of accounts. Surveys, fake doors and A/B tests need traffic that a young B2B product rarely has.

A ladder of 5 rungs rising in evidence strength: past behavior (analytics, tickets) → what they say (interviews) → what many say (one-question survey) → what they click (fake door) → what they pay (pricing test). Side label 'attitudinal → behavioral'. Text panel: ordered list.

One index card with 4 labeled fields filled for a hypothetical AI shift-swap suggestion in a B2B scheduling SaaS (we believe / to verify we will / and measure / we are right if), with a 'set before launch' stamp. Text panel: 4-line list. Label 'hypothetical' on the card.

Scatter plot: x = cost and effort (low → high), y = strength of evidence (weak → strong); 14 labeled dots; a bracket marking the design sprint bundle (prototype + 5-user test); an arrow 'run upward and rightward only after a pass'. Not a quadrant card (the sibling used a 4-quadrant risk card). Text panel: table technique | cost | evidence | run it when.

Four trays side by side (task mapping, use-case ranking, concept, test), each holding technique chips from the matrix; small 'days' label on each tray from the hub (1–2, 3–4, 5–7, 8–10). Not a timeline bar. Text panel: table step | techniques it runs | output.

CASE STUDIES (exact facts only): Mass Media Co.: 'We began with a discovery workshop, because the redesign had to serve MMC's business goals first. Stakeholders and end users joined us to define the product, set the strategy, and map the information architecture and user flows.' Results (if quoted, as stated): order processing efficiency +30%; error rate from 25% to 2+. TradeZella: 'We started with discovery and ended with trader testing. Stakeholder sessions first showed us TradeZella's long-term vision'; user flows redrawn around the widgets and features traders open most; 'traders tested it before it went live'. Results: +40% user interaction, +25% retention, +30% new customers. Never attribute a result to one technique. Do NOT use Digno, Vocable (sibling used them) or Nitro. No case study lists this hub: do not call either one 'an AI discovery workshop project'.

DO NOT USE: '5 users find 85% of problems' unless the fact-checker finds it on the NN/g page; 'about 50 participants per tree test' unless the NN/g page states it; any vendor click-through benchmark for fake doors; any '% of features are rarely used' statistic; Productboard or UserTesting survey numbers; the Rework '500 teams' figure about Torres.

DO NOT MIRROR: plane.so's risk-by-risk method lists and its 'teams gravitate toward usability' line; heymarvin's generic sequence (research → framing → competitors → personas → prototyping → sprints); decode.agency's 'brainstorming first' order; any numbered 'N techniques' H2 list.

ENTITY SALIENCE: 'product discovery techniques' exact 10–13 uses; H2s 1, 4, 6 and 8 carry the exact phrase (4 of 9 = 44%), and all 9 carry 'techniques' or a keyword word for the on-page script. Rival entities capped at about 6 uses each: 'prototype', 'interview', 'risk', 'AI', 'fake door'. 'product discovery' alone (sibling keyword) at most 5 uses outside the exact phrase.

VOICE: first person by Sahar Asif for method and judgment ('When a team brings me an AI idea, I ask which risk is still open…'). 'We' only for hub, home.ts and case-study facts. Every number not in eav is either method stated as 'I' or dropped. Hypotheticals labeled ('Say you run a scheduling app for US clinics…'). American spelling; US examples.

HONESTY: the fake door FAQ and section must say the follow-up page discloses that the feature is not built; never suggest collecting payment for a feature that does not exist. Wizard of Oz: say participants are told afterward.
